starter-templates.plain: Choose a starter game and the language that owns its gameplay rules.
starter-templates.analogy: The same level and actors can take their directions from three different scripts.
flow: Open the generated scene and press Play
details: Six templates are available in each authoring language.
The other two language systems remain available for additional classes.
Lua starter code is compiled to native C++ for PSX.
starter-templates.tip: Inspect the generated classes to see how each language connects to the same scene.

dungeon-complete.plain: Explore Reactor Station, the complete third-person action game shipped with Epok.
dungeon-complete.analogy: A finished game gives you a working project to take apart room by room.
flow: Play, then inspect the scene and rules
details: The template includes combat, a boss, upgrades, inventory, saving and a PocketStation companion.
C++, Blueprint and Lua variants share the same scene and assets.
A self-contained PSX disc uses CD on demand.
dungeon-complete.tip: The browser demo lets you try the PSX game before creating a project.

gameplay-controls.plain: Use named gameplay actions and temporary contexts to route controller input.
gameplay-controls.analogy: A menu can borrow the controller while it is open and hand it back when it closes.
flow: Push a context for a mode
Read the actions and release the context
details: Contexts determine which actions are active.
Higher-priority contexts can consume a shared input.
The same action layer is available to C++, Blueprints and Lua.
gameplay-controls.tip: Release a temporary context when its UI closes or its owner is removed.

world-gameplay-helpers.plain: Place reflected gameplay actors for common world interactions.
world-gameplay-helpers.analogy: Start with a working door or pickup, then give it your own rules.
flow: Test its interaction in the scene
details: The helpers cover examination, dialogue, pickups, doors and switches.
Derived classes can add rules in any supported gameplay language.
Interactions use the same runtime objects as the rest of the scene.
world-gameplay-helpers.tip: Start with the helper whose existing behavior matches your interaction.

dialogue-widgets.plain: Separate conversation content from the UI class that presents it.
dialogue-widgets.analogy: A dialogue asset holds the script and the widget stages it.
flow: Choose or derive a presenter widget
details: A presenter is a UIActor derived from DialoguePresenter.
Conversation assets contain lines, choices, conditions and actions.
Dialogue can use its own input context while active.
dialogue-widgets.tip: Test the transition back to gameplay when a conversation ends.

character-motor.plain: Feed movement commands into the shared 2D or 3D character motor.
character-motor.analogy: The controller supplies a direction and the motor handles moving through the level.
flow: Tune and test against level collision
details: The motors handle bounded collision and grounded movement.
2D and 3D use their respective world and collision data.
Gameplay classes can drive the motor from input or game rules.
character-motor.tip: Test movement on the slopes and platforms the player will actually encounter.

character-animation.plain: Connect movement and gameplay state to character animation playback.
character-animation.analogy: The same character can choose a walk, fall or action clip based on its current state.
details: Animation behavior is shared across starter languages.
Movement and gameplay provide signals for clip selection.
Animation costs remain subject to target budgets.
character-animation.tip: Check interruptions and changes of direction as well as steady movement.

camera-rigs.plain: Use gameplay camera rigs to follow and frame a character or scene.
camera-rigs.analogy: A rig gives the camera a job and constraints rather than a fixed transform.
details: Camera behavior and projection have shared helpers.
The selected camera still determines the rendered view.
The guide documents the options and bounds of each rig.
camera-rigs.tip: Check the camera near walls and in tight turns.

health.plain: Store and update bounded health with shared gameplay functions.
health.analogy: A health gauge can fill or drain only within its defined range.
details: HealthState stores values and HealthLibrary supplies shared operations.
Health arithmetic is bounded.
Gameplay classes decide how to display damage or handle defeat.
health.tip: Keep game-specific death and retry behavior in your gameplay class.

projectiles.plain: Reuse a bounded pool to fire and update 3D projectiles.
projectiles.analogy: Each shot borrows a slot and returns it when its flight ends.
flow: Handle hits and size the pool
details: ProjectilePool3DComponent owns the shared pool.
The component uses the existing 3D collision backend.
Pool capacity sets how many projectiles can be active together.
projectiles.tip: Test simultaneous shots in a representative combat encounter.

spatial-query-context.plain: Share a context for gameplay queries against the 3D world.
spatial-query-context.analogy: Nearby systems use one map to ask what is in their path or reach.
flow: Connect the systems that use it
Run a query and inspect its results
details: SpatialQueryContextComponent wraps existing 3D collision queries.
The helper is available through the shared gameplay layer.
Query results depend on the configured geometry and filters.
spatial-query-context.tip: Check collision layers when a query misses an expected target.

actors.plain: Actors are the objects in a map; components give each one its spatial and gameplay behavior.
actors.analogy: A door is an Actor; its transform and sound are components working together.
details: 3D, 2D and UI Actors have distinct spatial roots.
Logical parenting and spatial attachment are separate.
Previous Entity/Behaviour projects must be recreated for the current architecture.
actors.tip: Use the class picker and Inspector to check which components are compatible.

migration-actors.plain: Older Entity/Behaviour projects need to be recreated for the current Actor architecture.
migration-actors.analogy: Treat the old project as a source archive while rebuilding its map in the new format.
flow: Copy source assets and recreate maps and gameplay
details: Legacy Entity/Behaviour maps and old Blueprint versions are rejected rather than converted.
Maps use one Actor collection with transforms on spatial root components.
There is no automatic migration layer.
migration-actors.tip: Keep the original project and its source assets until the recreated version has been verified.

worlds-2d.plain: Build 2D worlds with sprites, tile maps, cameras, collision, animation and gameplay alongside a 3D world or UI.
worlds-2d.analogy: A side-scrolling character lives in the world; a health bar lives on the screen.
flow: Create a 2D node or Platformer template
Build and check the console output
details: World2D uses pixel units with Y pointing down.
TileSet and TileMap tools support authored 2D environments.
Under 3D canvases and Depth2D masks can combine 2D backgrounds with a 3D scene.
worlds-2d.tip: Check the target output when mixing 2D and 3D, because the PSX sorts whole triangles.

dungeon-template.plain: The Dungeon starter combines procedural level generation with a playable example.
dungeon-template.analogy: A reusable set of rooms and rules creates a different floor from a seed.
details: Recipes control rooms, branches, locks and other layout rules.
Generated content and gameplay still have bounded console budgets.
Dungeon Complete is a separate finished action-game template.
dungeon-template.tip: Keep the seed when reporting a generation issue so the same layout can be reproduced.

dungeons.plain: The dungeon tools assemble levels from authored rooms and generation rules.
dungeons.analogy: A recipe tells the generator which room pieces to connect.
details: Recipes support branches, loops, keys, locks and floors.
Generated results can be previewed and queried by gameplay.
The runtime and renderer remain subject to project budgets.
dungeons.tip: Start with a small recipe before adding complex constraints.

terrain.plain: Terrain tools let you sculpt a heightfield and paint its materials in the editor.
terrain.analogy: Shape a landscape, then paint where each ground material belongs.
flow: Build and test its collision and rendering
details: Heightfield resolution and materials affect the generated console data.
Collision depends on the selected terrain setup.
Complexity must fit PSX memory and frame budgets.
terrain.tip: Test the target result while increasing terrain detail.

lua-scripting.plain: Write gameplay classes in Lua and select a supported execution mode for the project.
lua-scripting.analogy: Lua describes an Actor's behavior using the engine's typed gameplay services.
flow: Build and test on the chosen target
details: Gameplay profiles define supported language and API behavior.
Project settings select native compilation or the supported VM modes.
Lua access is bounded by the exposed gameplay API.
lua-scripting.tip: Use the language-specific diagnostics and API guide when a script fails to compile.

gameplay-api.plain: The gameplay API provides shared services to C++, Blueprint and supported Lua gameplay.
gameplay-api.analogy: A common control panel exposes the game services each language can call.
flow: Check its contract and target limits
details: API availability depends on language and Lua profile.
Object references and runtime resources have bounded lifetimes.
Use the native API reference for exact C++ signatures.
gameplay-api.tip: Check the documented profile and return status when a call is unavailable or fails.

navigation.plain: NavLite provides bounded navigation for supported 3D gameplay.
navigation.analogy: A walking graph gives an NPC routes through a level instead of guessing where floors connect.
details: The walking graph is generated from supported scene geometry.
Search work is bounded for the target.
Review the guide for supported surfaces and update behavior.
navigation.tip: Inspect the baked graph before tuning an NPC's movement.

data-tables.plain: Asset DataTables map stable keys to typed asset references for gameplay.
data-tables.analogy: A sound-effects table is a labeled shelf of clips that gameplay can look up by name.
details: References use persistent asset identity.
C++, Blueprints and supported Lua can look up assets.
Table edits require a rebuild to update a running game.
data-tables.tip: Choose stable row keys and check missing-reference diagnostics before building.

video.plain: Import and play full-screen video using PlayStation MDEC video and XA audio.
video.analogy: A cutscene streams from disc while the game temporarily gives the screen to the player.
flow: Build with a supported CD data path
details: Import converts the source to a console video stream.
Playback pauses gameplay and can be skippable.
CD streaming and platform-specific import requirements apply.
video.tip: Read the current platform validation notes before relying on video import in a release workflow.

pocketstation.plain: Create PocketStation programs and connect them to a PlayStation game.
pocketstation.analogy: The memory-card device is a small companion computer with its own screen and buttons.
flow: Build and debug it in the device window
details: Pocket Lua compiles to ARM; ARM/Thumb assembly is also supported.
The editor provides an emulated device and debugger.
C++, Blueprints and Lua can install, start and exchange data with apps.
pocketstation.tip: The emulated Play link uses memory-card slot 1; check the guide for hardware workflow details.

scene-files.plain: Move selected cooked scene data out of the executable and load it when a scene starts.
scene-files.analogy: Several rooms take turns using one shared shelf instead of all occupying it at once.
details: External scenes use SCENEnn.BIN files and a shared memory region.
Engine code and scripts remain in the executable.
The selected CD or PC data path must supply the files.
scene-files.tip: Measure transition behavior and the shared region required by the largest external scene.

ps-exe-export.plain: Export a PlayStation executable and any required companion files for supported loaders.
ps-exe-export.analogy: Package the game together with the data its loading method expects.
flow: Run it with a compatible loader
details: A PS-X EXE is distinct from a disc image.
External scene or geometry data may require companion files.
Loader and data-source compatibility determine what can run.
ps-exe-export.tip: Check the package manifest and test the exact loading method you intend to distribute.

world-optimization.plain: Measure and tune scene costs using Epok's bounded rendering and visibility tools.
world-optimization.analogy: Find the expensive rooms before spending time optimizing the entire building.
details: Visibility, streaming and prepared rendering have different use cases.
Memory and frame budgets constrain each technique.
An enabled optimization does not guarantee faster rendering.
world-optimization.tip: Keep a comparable baseline capture before changing settings.

code-editor.plain: Edit project Lua and C++ inside Epok's integrated code workspace.
code-editor.analogy: A script tree and tabbed editor sit beside the rest of the game project.
flow: Edit and save a source file
details: Lua Language Server and clangd provide optional language assistance.
External file changes are checked before saving.
Copilot is optional and requires its own account entitlement.
code-editor.tip: Use the Problems panel to navigate to source diagnostics.

texture-cooking.plain: Texture cooking converts authored texture packages into indexed data and VRAM placements for PSX builds.
texture-cooking.analogy: The cook packs texture pages and palettes into the console's limited graphics memory.
details: Eligible indexed textures use 4-bit or 8-bit data.
Pixel rectangles and palettes are packed into VRAM deterministically.
A build reports placements that do not fit.
texture-cooking.tip: Check the cooked result and VRAM budget when changing texture density or palettes.

camera-space.plain: Camera-space rendering uses different numeric representations for world positions, chunk-local geometry and projection.
camera-space.analogy: Keep the camera's map location separate from the small coordinates the console uses to project nearby geometry.
details: World translations and local vertices use distinct fixed-point representations.
Near and far clipping are relative to the camera.
The GTE has bounded projection input and precision.
camera-space.tip: Check the representation and scale of each stage when debugging distant geometry.

formats.plain: Epok projects contain authored documents, generated output and local preferences with distinct ownership.
formats.analogy: Treat maps and asset packages as project source, and generated build files as outputs.
flow: Edit it with its owning tool
details: Maps, project settings and source assets have different formats and owners.
The current Actor architecture rejects older Entity/Behaviour maps instead of silently converting them.
Generated build data and local preferences should not be mistaken for authored assets.
formats.tip: Keep older projects intact when recreating their content in the current format.

skeletal.plain: Import FBX characters and compile rigid or baked-vertex animation for PlayStation.
skeletal.analogy: A small hierarchy of bones and sampled poses gives a low-polygon character movement.
flow: Choose a target animation format and test
details: Direct rigid skinning and compressed baked vertex frames share the same authoring pipeline.
Material slots can use imported textures.
Blended weights, animation blending, retargeting and root-motion extraction remain outside the current profile.
skeletal.tip: Measure the target workload when choosing between the two animation formats.

mcp.plain: MCP lets a compatible client inspect and operate the open Epok project through an optional local integration.
mcp.analogy: A client uses explicit editor operations instead of reaching into project state unchecked.
details: Tools cover scene editing, project assets, captures, builds and Play.
Mutation operations validate their inputs and revision contracts.
The server is off by default; see the guide for its current capabilities and connection settings.
mcp.tip: Capture and inspect the result after a visual change.

runtime-services.plain: Runtime services coordinate scenes, object lifetimes and bounded gameplay helpers.
runtime-services.analogy: A stage manager handles scene changes while each Actor follows its own lifecycle.
details: Actors and components use begin_play, tick and end_play.
External scene files and geometry streaming have separate data and memory contracts.
Resolve object identities before use and check queued work after scene teardown.
runtime-services.tip: Use current Actor templates when writing new gameplay and validate the exact loading path.
